Review of “
                The philanthropy's crucial role in alleviating stunting in Indonesia through research funding: A policy brief”, in F1000, by René Bekkers, 
                r.bekkers@vu.nl

5 October 2024

This policy paper recommends major legal and policy changes in the allocation of research-development expenditure in Indonesia to create a more supportive environment for philanthropy, which will reduce stunting.

Title

The title of the article is unclear. It could be read as an empirical statement, claiming that philanthropy has had a critical influence in the reduction of stunting. The title could also be read as an encouragement. If indeed this is the impression that the manuscript attempts to create, the title should be revised accordingly.

Abstract

The claim in the first sentence of the Background section that evidence is lacking “especially in stunting research” is not supported by an analysis or reference to previous research. If such previous research exists it should be cited. If it does not exist, replacing “especially” by “including” could save the sentence. The second sentence talks about a “short policy”. It is not clear what a “short policy” means. Perhaps a “short policy paper” is meant?

The claim in the Policy and Implications section that increases in R&D budgets in Singapore and Thailand and supportive environments for philanthropy “prove that evidence-based and practical researches can lead to the reduction of estimated prevalence of stunting rather than innovation-stage research” implies a distinction between “evidence-based and practical researches” on the one hand and “innovation-stage research” on the other. The data analyzed in the manuscript do not contain categorizations, measures or analyses of these two types of research. Ideally, the manuscript would clearly define the two types of research and operationalize them in concrete measures for which data are provided. If such data are not available, the statement could be reformulated without the distinction in the form of a suggestion, for instance as “increases in R&D budgets and philanthropic funding can reduce stunting”.

The claim in the Recommendations section that “changes in law and policy which regulate the allocation of research-development expenditure [which] will initiate the creation of a supportive environment for philanthropy acts regarding stunting” is formulated as a hypothesis about the future. This claim could be reformulated as a suggestion, replacing “will” by “together with”.

Introduction

The statement that “Philanthropic activities are now considered as strategic giving with an integrated and patterned goal” is unclear because it is a passive sentence that does not identify who is considering philanthropy. The references (Van Aaken & Buchner, 2020; Saiia et al., 2003) in the manuscript to support this statement are studies on corporate social responsibility and corporate philanthropy in the US, respectively. The statement could be rewritten as “Scholarship increasingly analyses corporate philanthropy and corporate social responsibility as strategic behaviors”.

The statement that “the environmental gap that supports the implementation of philanthropy activities (known as the global philanthropy environment index) in Southeast Asian countries” is unclear. It could be rewritten to state that “In 2018, countries in Southeast Asia (Myanmar, Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Singapore) had relatively low scores on the global philanthropy environment index measuring the favorability of conditions for philanthropy.”

The region score (not weighted by population) for Southern and Southeastern Asia was 3.30. The (unweighted) global average score was 3.64.

The GPEI data analyzed refer to 2018. Meanwhile, a new edition is published for 2022,
                https://globalindices.indianapolis.iu.edu/environment-index/regions/southern-southeastern-asia/index.html

By 2022 the regional average for Southern and Southeastern Asia had increased somewhat to 3.41, while the global average remained about the same (3.63).

Policy and Implications

This section seems to argue that efforts to reduce stunting can be made more effective by philanthropic funding for research. The current manuscript does not clearly discuss the arguments supporting this conjecture. It contains two components: 1) interventions based on evidence from research are more effective than interventions not based on research; 2) philanthropic funding for research provides research evidence.

This section would benefit from an analysis of the sources of funding that could contribute to achieve the policy goal of reducing stunting. What proportion of funding comes from philanthropic sources?

The evidence cited to support the claim that “Recent evidence found that charitable funding plays a crucial role in funding research, which showed philanthropic foundations, trusts, and charities as an important source of research funding” is not so recent at all. More recent research could be cited to support the statement, for example:

Shekhtman, L. M., Gates, A. J., & Barabási, A. L. (2024). Mapping philanthropic support of science. 
                    Scientific Reports, 
                    14(1), 9397. (1)

In the sentence mentioning “A new analysis of a few South-East Asian countries” a reference to the (allegedly new) analysis should be included.

“The acceleration of the stunting reduction programs has reduced the prevalence of stunting.” is a causal statement, the basis of which is not clear. It is not justified by the evidence presented in the current manuscript. To make such a claim, evidence from RCTs in field or natural settings would be ideal. Other research designs that could justify such a claim involve a comparison of stunting outcome data from a program delivering treatment to some individuals with a control group of otherwise comparable individuals who did not receive treatment. It is not clear how the claim is supported by the data reported in the manuscript. The manuscript could cite the Executive Report Accelerating the Reduction of Stunting for the Year 2022 as a source of data, though it does not provide a description of a research design that could justify a causal claim.

The manuscript mentions several objectives of a presidential decree (“improve the quality of preparation for family life, ensure the fulfilment of nutritional intake, improve parenting, improve access and quality of health services, and improve access to drinking water and sanitation”), but it is not clear how these objectives are related to stunting. Are they means to the end of reducing stunting?

Furthermore, it is not clear which programs or interventions are implemented to reduce stunting in Indonesia. How are these efforts related to breastfeeding and birth weight? The manuscript mentions five pillars, two of which are identified. However, it is not clear which pillar is “the pillar mentioned”. Also it is not clear which pillar is meant in the sentence describing that researchers can contribute to “one of the strategic pillars”.

The sentence “However, the prevalence raised to 37.2 in 2013% but eventually reduced to 30.8% in 2018.” is somewhat confusing. Rewriting it and providing a visual illustration of the data in the form of a line graph could help. It is not clear what “treatment coverage” refers to.

The justification for the claim that “the utilization of research to address the problem seems to be below the expected levels” is unclear. It could be clarified by explaining who held which expectations, and providing data on the actual use of research.

Percutaneous ultrasound/CT guided drainage procedures are considered safe and effective, although it is an under-utilised technique in many parts of the world. Success of CT-guided percutaneous drainage is related to proper patient selection, preparation and adequate procedural planning and experience and skills of a performing physician. The article describes the experience and outcome of procedures performed on several groups of patients with different indications and location of collections. The article touches on intermittent needle aspiration and percutaneous drainage and importance of re-assessing the collections for adequate drainage and looking at any associated complications.

The article could have touched more upon different types of drainage catheters and different drainage technique for complex collections and collections at difficult locations and their approach. It was good to know the study hasn’t demonstrated any major complications with percutaneous drainages performed suggesting these are safe and effective procedures.

Congratulations to all the authors involved.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard.

The authors are to be commended for raising a practical issue which needs resolution in the “Time of Covid”. I take this to be the need to satisfactorily prove the witnessing of conveyancing documents when, under covid conditions, person-to-person meetings are not permissible.

The article opens with a broad discussion of legal issues related to signatures and attestation. The authors recognise that, in essence, a signature is some physical “affixing” to a document showing an intention to be bound. They acknowledge that, at law, a signature may be an inked thumb print, an “e-signature” or even a “digital signature”. They also record the purpose of the Digital Signatures Act 1997 (DSA) and the Electronic Commerce Act 2006 (ECA) which, in combination, may enable a “digital” signature to be accepted for evidential purposes, providing certain statutory protocols are adhered to. The article then extends on to mention to other issues in practice, such as some government agencies only accepting signatures made in “black fountain wet-ink”. The authors reflect that, welcome as the provisions in the DSA and ECA are, those provisions do not adequately extend to situations where execution must be undertaken before a witness who is not physically present under covid conditions.

This last point I take to be the central issue that the article ultimately seeks to address, although this is not clear because of the preceding, rather general discussion. The question then posed, appears to be whether execution of conveyancing documents can be understood to be “before” a witness who is only available by an electronic link. The conclusion in the abstract is representative of the broad ranging discussion that has occurred. It reads as follows.

“Thus, it is suggested that there is a need for a unique legal framework for e-signature and attestation in Malaysia due to the lack of specific laws which govern the issue of electronic signature and attestation”.

It seems to me that the article would have benefited from isolating out, and then starting with the key issue to be addressed.  As stated, I take this to be the present need for conveyancing documents to be signed before witnesses who are physically present. The material presented could then be better positioned to discuss possible solutions. Mention of the requirements of the DSA and ECA do have their place, but only in the sense of identifying missed opportunities.

By the time I got to the conclusion, I was made aware of the problem, but was unclear on the solution. On the one hand the authors seem to suggest “e-signatures are a viable solution”, notwithstanding their recognition that for e-signatures, “safety factors” remain a concern.  At the same time they suggest the ECA be “amended to allow conveyancing solicitors to attest the signing of a document via video conferencing platform[s]”.

In essence, I was left a little uncertain whether the purpose of the article was to identify all legal issues related to electronic signatures, or to discuss  possible solutions for signatures to conveyancing documents that must be signed before a witness. The two topics are interrelated, but different.

The authors are to be commended for taking the first step into the arena. We all benefit from a discussion such as this.
